title: Due diligence: Configuration drives extraction performance
desc: Finds model choice and follow-up prompts alter provision-level results, making aggregate generative-AI rankings insufficient.

kps.k: Legal due-diligence extraction performance depends on the configuration, not simply on whether a tool uses generative AI.
kps.d: The RAG Report: Large Language Models in Legal Due Diligence finds that its improved-prompt RAG 10 GPT4-32K configuration leads the tested alternatives, with average F1 scores of 0.92 initially and 0.95 after follow-up prompting. The machine-learning extraction tool scores 0.86, while the GenAI contract-review tool scores 0.72. This supports a task-specific case for tailored retrieval-augmented generation, rather than a general claim that generative tools outperform conventional software. The experiment measures provision extraction, not legal advice quality or readiness for autonomous due diligence.

kps.k: Model choice and follow-up prompting materially change the results.
kps.d: The authors report a 9.2% average improvement from follow-up prompting across configurations. In their matched RAG 10 comparison, GPT4-32K improves on GPT4-Turbo by a reported 4% for initial prompts and 1% for follow-ups across all provisions; excluding Effective Date and Governing Law raises those figures to 7% and 2%. These are the report's stated percentage improvements. The practical implication is to test the full prompting workflow and model configuration rather than infer performance from a model or product label.

kps.k: Aggregate rankings conceal substantial differences between provision types.
kps.d: The tested in-context configuration achieves 1.00 F1 for Effective Date and Governing Law, but initially scores only 0.29 for Cap on Liability. The improved-prompt GPT4-32K follow-up reaches 0.95 on Cap on Liability. Conversely, the machine-learning tool matches GPT4-Turbo RAG follow-ups on Assignment at 0.95. These within-study contrasts qualify any blanket superiority claim and favour provision-level testing when selecting tools and setting review procedures. The supplied material presents no separate opposing source; the principal qualification comes from the report's own heterogeneous results.

kps.k: Observed failures support attention to customisation, but do not establish why particular systems succeed or fail.
kps.d: The authors observe that the machine-learning tool struggles with long, unusually structured, agreement-specific and page-spanning provisions. They interpret stronger LLM extraction as greater conceptual understanding and flexibility, rather than independently measuring understanding. The GenAI review tool paraphrases instead of extracting verbatim, gives partial citations and short answers, and responds inconsistently. The authors suggest that non-adjustable system prompts and model parameters probably explain these failures, but do not establish causation. For deployment, the findings favour testing instruction adherence, extraction completeness and citation quality alongside average F1, and assessing whether teams can adjust the workflow.

vlens.an: The traditional-practice source supports the proposition that due-diligence extraction performance is configuration- and task-dependent rather than an inherent consequence of using generative AI. Its evidence shows that follow-up prompting improves average results and that model choice changes performance in a matched RAG workflow. The source also reinforces the proposition’s warning against aggregate rankings: outcomes vary materially by provision, and a conventional machine-learning tool matches some RAG configurations on Assignment despite the tailored GPT4-32K RAG setup leading overall. This is internal variation within one experimental report, not evidence of disagreement among law firms or of prevalence across traditional practice. The source further distinguishes observed failures—such as weak instruction adherence and incomplete extraction—from its tentative explanation that non-adjustable system settings caused them.

elens.an: The supplied 2023–2024 source supports the proposition that due-diligence provision extraction is configuration-dependent and cannot be judged reliably from an aggregate generative-AI label or ranking. Its experiments report that follow-up prompting improves average performance and that, in a matched RAG comparison, GPT4-32K outperforms GPT4-Turbo. Material internal variation reinforces rather than undermines that conclusion: results differ by provision type, the leading tailored RAG configuration is not superior on every provision, and the weakest generative-AI tool exhibits instruction-following and extraction-quality failures. The evidence is limited to provision extraction in this particular study; it does not establish the quality of legal advice, readiness for autonomous due diligence, or the proposed causal explanation that non-adjustable system settings produced the weaker tool’s failures. Because the corpus supplies one curated source for this period, this assessment characterises that source rather than broader opinion or prevalence.
